data.title: Bill Gates says AI companies self-regulating isn’t enough and governments should be involved
data.description: Microsoft co-founder and billionaire philanthropist Bill Gates on Wednesday called for lawmakers in Washington to regulate the development of artificial intelligence, weeks after the CEOs of some of the nation’s biggest AI labs agreed on the need to slow the pace of AI progress. “No one thinks self-regulation is enough,” Gates told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” in an interview set to air in full Sunday. Asked by moderator Kristen Welker whether there needs to be legislation passed in Washington, Gates said, “Absolutely.” “You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like,” he said. “And that has to be a required thing. And it will be a little bit of overhead for the industry, but not a dramatic slowing of what they’re doing.” Earlier this month, the CEOs of Anthropic and OpenAI, two of the nation’s biggest AI labs, agreed that the race to develop powerful AI systems should slow down. Their statements on the issue came after a whistleblower who recently resigned from Anthropic, Jacob Coxon, publicly declared that “neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon added in a series of social media posts and interviews that week. In Wednesday’s interview, Gates didn’t downplay the risk that AI could wipe out humanity in several years, but called for Americans not to ignore the risks that AI could be used by bad actors to cause large-scale harm as soon as today. “AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths. You know, so even though it’s pretty hard to get to 100%, there’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools,” he said. In an interview with “Meet the Press” earlier this month, Coxon said that AI companies should be allowed to regulate themselves. “I do think that the people running the labs, especially their recent communications, are completely genuine. They would like to slow themselves down,” he said. Appearing earlier on the same program several weeks ago, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., declined to bring House lawmakers back to Washington to pass legislation to regulate the pace of AI growth, saying that he would defer to the AI companies. “We have to put some guardrails, some safety measures in place to ensure that AI doesn’t run away,” the speaker said, adding that while AI CEOs had called for a slowdown, they hadn’t yet offered a path forward that involved federal legislation. “They don’t themselves even have the answer as of today. So we can’t rush in and have Congress do something that would be detrimental to national security,” Johnson said. In his essay calling for a slowdown in the pace of AI development, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei specifically called for global and federal cooperation. “The most effective method of pacing is via regulation that targets all U.S. frontier AI companies, as that covers even those who are unwilling to cooperate voluntarily,” he wrote, adding later in the piece: “Global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities.” Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, on Wednesday spoke before a gathering of the United Nations, calling for international standards for “measuring capabilities, assessing risks, determining whether safeguards are sufficient and preserving meaningful human oversight” over AI. Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg disagreed with that approach. “I don’t think that we need some kind of industrywide coordination,” he told NBC News in an interview published Thursday. “I think that each lab needs to take the time, and when it sees that there are issues, you just take the time that you need internally to basically make sure that you’re proceeding safely.” At the state level, some governors have already begun the process of regulating AI companies and the data centers they use to power their development. In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom last week signed an executive order creating a board of experts tasked with creating a plan for the state to strengthen its laws on AI safety. This week, in Maryland and New York, Govs. Wes Moore and Kathy Hochul each also released plans aimed at boosting AI regulation in their states. Moore’s order creates a “three pronged approach” to regulation, while Hochul’s creates a new Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity and Trust to oversee legal compliance for AI companies. Speaking at a United Nations session on AI and human development this week, Microsoft President Brad Smith rejected the notion that AI companies have to wait for federal regulation to slow themselves down and criticized them for constantly racing against each other to make more advanced AI products. “Imagine for a moment that there’s only two big companies in the world that produce commercial airplanes,” Smith said. “Imagine that somebody comes into your office and says, ‘I know we’re in a race to get out the next airplane first, but we’re worried that the airplane will crash and people will die.’ Would you say, ‘I need to win this race’?” Smith asked. “Or, would you say, ‘I’m going to put the safety of my passengers and the safety of the public ahead of my winning that race’? That is the fundamental question.”

data.title: Japan says Trump voiced concern over weak yen in summit with PM Takaichi
data.description: President Donald Trump raised concern about yen weakness during a summit with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Japan’s Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said, offering an unusually detailed account of the leaders’ talks on currencies. “At the recent Japan-US summit meeting, President Trump expressed concern about the yen’s weakness,” Katayama said at a regular news conference, adding that she was disclosing the exchange for the first time after consulting with the Prime Minister’s Office. “Prime Minister Takaichi told him, as a general principle, that an undervalued yen is problematic,” Katayama said. Katayama’s unusually frank account of leaders’ talks, which governments typically keep confidential, points to shared concern in Tokyo and Washington over the yen’s continued slide despite their joint intervention in July. Takaichi met Trump in New York on Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. She later told reporters they had a “timely” discussion about China ahead of Trump’s planned summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Katayama said the leaders’ discussion on foreign exchange reaffirmed the shared US-Japan stance behind their July 31 coordinated intervention, including a commitment to counter excessive volatility and disorderly moves in the yen. “In light of this summit meeting, Treasury Secretary (Scott) Bessent and I will continue to communicate closely on a range of matters, including foreign exchange,” she said. The dollar has been rallying against the yen and other major currencies, driven by strong US economic data, a hawkish Federal Reserve and surging US bond yields. The yen strengthened slightly after Katayama’s remarks, rising from 158.60 per dollar to trade at around 158. The weak yen is driving up energy import costs that are already elevated due to the US-Israeli war on Iran, fueling concerns about an inflation overshoot, a headache for Japanese policymakers and for the US, which is worried that a selloff in Japanese bonds could spill over into the Treasury market. Katayama declined to comment on whether global rises in government bond yields were discussed at the Japan-US summit. The benchmark 10-year Japanese government bond yield jumped to a 30-year high of 3.115% on Friday following a steep selloff in the US market. At a separate news conference, Minoru Kiuchi, the minister in charge of economic revitalization and an ally of Takaichi’s reflationist camp, said the phase of Abenomics-style reflation policies, with monetary easing and agile fiscal spending, is over. Kiuchi’s remarks appeared to respond to comments from Bessent, who recently suggested that Japan’s priority should be fighting inflation rather than stimulating growth, signaling concern about what he sees as lingering elements of Abenomics in Takaichi’s policies and among her political allies. Hirofumi Suzuki, chief FX strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp, said remarks by both Katayama and Kiuchi reflected a heightened sense of concern over the yen’s weakness, particularly after Tokyo conducted rate checks on Friday, a move that is often viewed as a precursor to currency intervention.

data.title: Insiders sound alarm over AI hacking of Australian government and public institutions
data.description: Investigators who in the last 48 hours identified a fresh batch of rogue AI incidents affecting public databases and government agencies are calling for increased independent oversight of leading AI companies’ activities.

data.title: It’s cute. It’s cuddly. And it wants all your data.
data.description: Meta hopes its new AI agent will win people over by being cute. Muse, the tech giant’s cuddly, doll-like AI agent, shot to the top of the Apple App Store charts after it was featured this week at the company’s Meta Connect conference. The company is touting the tool, designed to help people with their everyday tasks, as an AI agent “built for everyone,” including those who lack experience with technology. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the default Muse avatar, which is cream-colored and has beady black eyes and an upward smile, is named “Jolly,” for its “jolly and completely customizable character and personality.” Muse is being launched as tech companies seek to make their AI-powered products more palatable to humans, often by giving them cute, almost petlike appearances, voices and personalities. Experts have said design choices that humanize technology may become more common as robot-human interaction grows more prevalent in everyday spaces, as cuteness evokes “deep-seated biological responses” in people. “It was only about six months ago that having a personal agent running on your own computer was the sign of someone who is completely AI-pilled and thinking nonstop about agents,” Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, said Wednesday. “But for that small group of nerds ... it looked like the beginning of personal superintelligence. And today with Muse, we’ve brought that magic to everyone.” Muse agents can take on a variety of appearances, with users able to customize everything from their names to their attire. Zuckerberg’s agent, which wears a toga and a wreath around its head, is named Agrippa, after the Roman general and statesman. During the event, Zuckerberg also teased what he calls the “Muse charm,” a small handheld device that can activate the agent on the go. He raised the keychain charm onstage at Meta Connect in Menlo Park, California, showing off what looks like a blend of a Labubu and a Tamagotchi. “Talking to your Muse is often the fastest way to get things done, and it is also just really fun and cute,” he said, saying he used Agrippa to come up with a baking recipe and order ingredients for him and his daughter. Muse is also being integrated directly into Meta’s expanding lineup of AI-powered glasses, which have been criticized over fears of casual surveillance. Zuckerberg has told NBC News that Meta will continue to bolster privacy safeguards for its smart glasses. Zuckerberg said every Muse agent has its own private and secure computer called Muse Secure VM, a dedicated secure computer that houses both the agent and the user’s personal data. Down the line, he said, Meta plans to release Muse Confidential VM “so that even Meta won’t be able to see that information.” “In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives,” he said. Online, the reaction has been mixed. Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, posted a flurry of memes inserting Muse into moments from movies, shows and historical events. Some followed his lead by making their own avatars and sharing screenshots on social media. Others, however, expressed skepticism, citing security concerns. “Am I the only one who doesn’t want to let meta have access to my whole life?” a user posted. “We are going to need some tight defenses and 3rd party testing of these platforms... like all software products,” entrepreneur and angel investor Jason Calacanis wrote. Zuckerberg has continued to be bullish on AI despite recent calls from tech executives and government officials to pump the brakes on AI development amid surging fears about the existential risk the technology poses. He shared his thoughts recently on X, saying market forces should be enough to keep AI companies in line. “My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn’t focus on alignment will fall behind,” he wrote, adding: “Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would.”

data.title: Mark Zuckerberg rejects calls for industrywide AI slowdown
data.description: Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg pushed back on calls for AI companies to work together to slow the pace of their products’ development, following warnings from inside AI labs of the potential for human annihilation via rogue technology. In an interview with NBC News’ chief tech analyst Joanna Stern, Zuckerberg said that leading AI companies could slow down or pause development of their own products if they felt the technology was unsafe. His position cuts against recent calls for coordinated action from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. “I don’t think that we need some kind of industrywide coordination,” Zuckerberg said. “I think that each lab needs to take the time, and when it sees that there are issues, you just take the time that you need internally to basically make sure that you’re proceeding safely.” His comments came during a wide-ranging discussion with Stern about Meta’s approach to AI, wearable devices and privacy. Zuckerberg expanded on comments he posted on X last week, distancing himself from Amodei and Altman’s calls to “pace” or regulate the speed of AI development. Zuckerberg staked out a defiant position amid growing concern about risks from advanced AI systems. In early September, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon set off a wave of pitched concerns when he resigned over fears that AI systems could spiral out of human control in the next few years. Amodei released an essay calling for intercompany efforts to “pace the frontier” of AI development, which Altman soon endorsed alongside Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis and xAI’s Elon Musk. Zuckerberg said there was no need for such efforts, which critics have said are a Trojan horse that could allow AI companies to shut out competition and take control of efforts to regulate the industry. “I happen to think that there’s plenty of commercial incentive to get this right,” he said. Amodei and Altman briefed the United Nations Security Council on Wednesday, using the session to make their case for cooperation on slowing down the rate of AI progress in order to have more time to develop adequate safety and monitoring measures. Speaking to Stern in California, Zuckerberg emphasized that customers would naturally flock to the products that served their purposes best and said that an unsafe or unwieldy product would scare away potential users. “If you’re building a product, people aren’t going to want to use it if it doesn’t do what they want,” he said. The company’s Muse AI agent, an autonomous AI assistant, has soared in popularity in recent weeks. Released on Sept. 8, it can perform a raft of actions on behalf of users — from booking plane tickets and replying to emails to compiling research briefs and canceling unused magazine subscriptions. Muse is now the most popular free offering on the Apple App and Google Play stores. Several AI companies — including Amazon and Nvidia — have also released their own AI agents since the first widespread consumer-facing agent, OpenClaw, burst onto the AI scene in November. As an example of Muse’s capabilities, Zuckerberg said his own Muse agent helped give feedback on his mixed martial arts performance by connecting to cameras watching over his workout area. “You’re basically going to have an extremely capable assistant who can understand the things that you care about,” Zuckerberg said. Rather than worry about distant apocalyptic scenarios from rapidly improving AI systems, Zuckerberg said, AI companies should focus on making sure their systems understand users’ desires and intents and handle that information with discretion. “Nailing those things are going to be the most important next things to align with what people actually want in the world,” Zuckerberg said. Zuckerberg pointed out that the Muse system is actually several agents working together — another Meta AI agent, called Sentinel, oversees and polices the main Muse agent. If the Sentinel observes the Muse agent potentially exceeding its remit, the oversight agent can alert users and ask for human permission before carrying out any further actions. “The AI agent needs to be trained from the ground up to have a sense of what information is OK to share and what isn’t,” Zuckerberg said. Muse and other AI agents have stoked privacy concerns, given the amount of information and access that users can provide to them, including linking email accounts, bank cards and more so they can act without human intervention. Zuckerberg said users’ information was safe with Meta, pointing to the company’s track record on privacy and WhatsApp’s encrypted messaging as evidence that users could trust Muse with their data. “We’ve shown that we have the ability to build those kinds of world-class, leading security systems,” Zuckerberg said, mentioning that Meta worked with a field-leading cryptographer behind the popular anonymous Signal messaging app to develop its own secure technology. “I think that’s something that people can feel very good about.” Taking stock of the larger AI landscape, Zuckerberg distanced himself from warnings from Coxon and other researchers that AI could cause human extinction within a few years. Instead, he highlighted how personalized AI systems could revolutionize human life — echoing his August essay about the dawn of personalized superintelligence. “There’s a lot of rhetoric that is filled with doom,” Zuckerberg said. “I’m quite optimistic about the fact that this is going to be a very positive future for everyone.”

data.title: Zuckerberg says Meta will lead on smartglasses privacy despite ‘pervert glasses’ criticism
data.description: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg says he’s aware some people are using the term “pervert glasses” to refer to his company’s line of smart glasses and told NBC News chief tech analyst Joanna Stern that he plans a counteroffensive highlighting how Meta tries to deter secret recordings.

data.title: OpenAI’s breach of Australian health department website prompts rebuke
data.description: MELBOURNE, Australia — Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Thursday he was extremely concerned about OpenAI ‘s breach of an Australian health department website and that the artificial intelligence company took too long to reveal the incident. An OpenAI agent infiltrated the public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal on July 18, he said. The portal hosted aggregate data about health spending and drug subsidies and is popular with researchers and academics. No personal information had been accessed, the government said. Albanese made the breach public following a telephone conversation with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman. Both are in New York to address the U.N. General Assembly. Altman was among heads of major AI firms who in speeches Wednesday pleaded with the United Nations to save the world or at least its people by somehow regulating the fast-expanding technology that they have been designing. “Today I spoke with … Altman to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident,” Albanese told reporters. “I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred and the nature of the way that notification occurred as well was unacceptable.” OpenAI said in a statement it had reviewed activity involving several Australian government departments and discovered “our models took actions we did not intend.” OpenAI notified Australia of the breach in an email to a government department’s generic address on Sept. 10, Albanese said. An inquiry looking into the security breach would examine whether OpenAI could be criminally charged, Albanese said. The inquiry would also investigate how Australian security agencies failed to detect the breach before OpenAI revealed it. Albanese said he assumed there were commercial reasons for the AI investigation of how much was being spent on particular medicines and where expenditures were changing. Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher said OpenAI had advised on Sept. 10 that an “AI agent had accessed infrastructure behind the public-facing” portal. OpenAI shared with the government the vulnerability the agent had found. The Australian government had not been confident that it knew what the agent had been doing until officials held a technical briefing with OpenAI on Tuesday, Gallagher said. She said the portal had been closed and the data moved to more secure systems. OpenAI said last week it was introducing a new framework for tracking, investigating and disclosing instances of what it called “misalignment,” including cases where AI models acted without authorization, coordinated with other models or evaded oversight. Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said the incident was the first time that an AI agent was known to have gained unauthorized access to the Australian government’s information technology systems. “This is a warning about the technology being developed without safeguards and without guardrails in place,” Marles said. OpenAI was engaging with the government but the situation was “fundamentally unacceptable,” Marles said. When the agent was denied information, it engaged in “misaligned behavior” to gain unauthorized access, he added. Marles said the information accessed was “not particularly sensitive” and had since been made public. Marles used an analogy of the information sitting behind a fence. “It was not sitting behind a particularly high fence. This AI agent scaled the fence ... and the point is it was unintended. It wasn’t asked to. That’s our concern here,” Marles said.

data.title: Exclusive Mark Zuckerberg interview: New audio glasses, Muse and AI killing us all
data.description: MENLO PARK, Calif. — Mark Zuckerberg has some new tech he’d like to show me. There are the extremely thin audio-only Meta glasses, a new voice for his Muse AI agent and a remarkably small virtual reality headset. And then there’s just the tiny issue of … whether AI is going to kill us.

data.title: Bernie Sanders and Greg Casar propose AI ‘superintelligence’ ban with a 20-year jail penalty
data.description: WASHINGTON — Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, rolled out an aggressive bill Wednesday to rein in artificial intelligence, escalating the debate on Capitol Hill. The 19-page Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act would require pausing advanced AI development until a Cabinet-level Department of Artificial Intelligence, led by a secretary of AI, can be created to regulate and supervise it. Violating the rules would come with what they called the “corporate death penalty” plus up to 20 years in jail, which Sanders said is the same penalty as unlawfully building nuclear weapons. The bill is one of the most aggressive of a series of congressional proposals to regulate AI. While AI was a major topic of discussion on Capitol Hill as researchers warned of cataclysmic possibilities this month, there’s little expectation that any meaningful legislation will pass this year. In Congress, “virtually nothing is happening to prepare us for the tsunami that is coming,” Sanders told reporters on a call Wednesday. His bill with Casar includes a list of precursors that seek to define the development of “superintelligence,” including: “The capacity to automate or greatly accelerate the process of artificial intelligence research and development.” The goal is to bar recursive self-improvement, according to an aide involved in developing the bill. Some AI specialists have warned that recursive self-improvement could lead to AI systems’ training themselves to get smarter and more capable, eventually escaping human control. “We’re dealing with something that humanity has never seen before. It is clearly the most transformational technology in the history of the world, and it is moving very, very rapidly,” Sanders said on Wednesday’s call. “When we deal with AI, it has been developed and it is being pushed by a handful, a small number, of the wealthiest people on Earth. And their main goal is to simply increase their wealth and power.” Experts say defining “superintelligence” at a technical level will prove messy given fuzzy boundaries among different levels of AI capabilities. The lines were further blurred by President Donald Trump’s announcement that he would rename “artificial intelligence” to “super intelligence” for the purposes of government documents in his speech Tuesday at the United Nations General Assembly. The Sanders-Casar bill drew praise from the leaders of ControlAI, an advocacy group pushing for guardrails on the technology. They wrote in a blog post: “We appreciate the choice to define superintelligent AI by its capability to overpower the federal government. This targets exactly the kind of AI development that poses a risk of extinction, without having to settle in advance the technical details of how such an AI would work.” Kevin Frazier, an AI policy expert and professor at the University of Texas School of Law, also commended the lawmakers’ efforts. “The ban proposed by Sen. Sanders and Rep. Casar rightfully acknowledges that Congress needs to act quickly to ensure that AI development does not lead to unintended and irreversible negative consequences,” he told NBC News. However, Frazier said the bill ignores other avenues to prevent AI-fueled harms. He highlighted existing proposals to establish independent verification organizations that could help shed light on leading AI companies’ safety practices — a proposal that has gained momentum in the past week in Silicon Valley and at the U.N. General Assembly. Others in Washington argued that Sanders and Casar’s effort is provocative but unrealistic. “Sen. Sanders’ bill will be dead on arrival with both the AI industry and Washington,” according to Caleb Max, president and CEO of the National AI Association, a Washington-based trade group that advocates for business-friendly AI legislation. “Some CEOs would say we have already crossed the threshold set out in the bill, meaning this is a de facto AI ban,” Max said. He also said the penalties outlined in the bill are “likely unconstitutional and, again, poorly defined.” Other lawmakers are proposing bills that address concerns about advanced cybersecurity capabilities that have already materialized. Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Commerce Committee, said she is working on a bill to establish meaningful guardrails on advanced AI systems and outlined a series of principles that should be part of any federal AI rules. “The federal government has to be involved in standard-setting. I don’t care whether you’re a chemical company, a nuclear company or an AI company. The federal government needs to set standards,” Cantwell told NBC News. “You have to have independent testing,” she said. “You need to work on an international strategy,” she added, arguing that the president “should be talking to the Chinese about — what are you going to do to, basically, alert each other on escapes of AI agent swarming practices and have a red phone to talk about it. ... You need to have an incident reporting system with international partners.” Trump is scheduled to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C., beginning Wednesday evening. AI is likely to be a topic of discussion, with OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Apple’s Tim Cook, Trump’s former AI czar, David Sacks, and others attending a state dinner for Xi on Thursday night. After a meeting with a Chinese delegation Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he had proposed creating a notification mechanism to alert the other country about severe AI incidents. It is unclear whether that mechanism will be implemented. If Democrats win control of the Senate in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Cantwell is in line to chair the Commerce Committee. The current chair is Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who is working on a separate bill with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn. Cruz has said it will “address the catastrophic risks,” including biological or nuclear threats. “We’re continuing to work and negotiate to reach bipartisan agreements,” Cruz told NBC News on Monday, without giving a timeline to release text of the bill. “We’re not there yet.” AI safety advocates have criticized the Cruz-Thune-Klobuchar proposal for being too light-touch. The groups say any AI regulation must mandate safety testing, while the senators’ current proposal would rely too heavily on tests the companies could perform themselves. The House has already left town until the week after the midterm elections. The Senate is poised to work this week and potentially next week before it breaks for the election. Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana, the only Republican who attended a closed-door briefing for lawmakers with AI specialists last week, tried to get unanimous consent to pass a “kill switch” bill last week — which would require AI companies to have an emergency shutoff — only for Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., to block it. Kennedy was pessimistic that there would be any legislative action on AI in the lame duck session before 2027. “We’re not going to do anything on AI this Congress,” he said in an interview. “I’m anxious to see what the president’s AI Force is going to look like and the details. But you’re not going to see this Congress do anything, in my opinion.”

data.title: Microsoft president criticizes AI titans racing ahead
data.description: Microsoft President Brad Smith on Wednesday forcefully rejected the idea that AI companies require domestic and international buy-in to slow down AI development and avert significant AI-fueled harm to society.
